Differential design and observations: the design matrix and every peptide, by mzLib

Source: vignettes/diff.Rmd
diff.Rmd

Before any differential test there are two tables to get right, and both are easy to get quietly wrong. The design: which coefficient means what, which level is the baseline, whether two things you want to separate can be separated by these samples at all. And the observations: what each peptide measured in each biological sample, with fractions summed and technical replicates averaged correctly, and a missing value kept as missing rather than written as 0.

diff_design() turns the sample sheet you already keep into mzLib’s design matrix, which equals R’s model.matrix(), and says which comparisons cannot be estimated and why. diff_observations() turns a FlashLFQ or MetaMorpheus peptide table into every peptide in every sample, as a log2 intensity or NA with the reason. Both write files that stats_fit() reads.

question function mzLib method
what is my design matrix, and which comparisons can these samples answer? diff_design() AnalysisDesign.ByStratum, .DefaultContrasts, .Estimability (#1450) treatment coding as R’s model.matrix() (Wilkinson and Rogers 1973)
what did each peptide measure in each sample, and if nothing, why? diff_observations() FlashLfqObservations.FromPeptideTable, ObservationTable (#1455) fractions summed, technical replicates averaged in log2
how far apart do the samples sit on the peptides they share? diff_observations() SharedPeptideNormalization.Measure, .Apply median of ratios to a geometric-mean reference (as Anders and Huber 2010)

Then test with stats_fit(): it reads the design file and the contrasts file diff_design() writes, and the responses file diff_observations() writes. See vignette("stats", package = "mzLibR").

From a sample sheet to a design

The differential-abundance article analyses a MALAT1 dilution series - 27 runs at 500, 250 or 125 ng - with a hand-made design of 0/1 columns. Here is the same experiment as a scientist writes it down: one row per run, and its load.

diff_data <- system.file("extdata", "diff", package = "mzLibR")
stats_data <- system.file("extdata", "stats", package = "mzLibR")
sheet <- read.delim(file.path(diff_data, "malat_dilution_samples.tsv"))
head(sheet, 3)
#>                                                             run malat_load
#> 1 2026_09_18_1MALAT_500ng_1FLuc_500ng_20mer-2_50ng_147mingrad-1      500ng
#> 2 2026_09_18_1MALAT_500ng_1FLuc_500ng_20mer-2_50ng_147mingrad-2      500ng
#> 3 2026_09_24_1MALAT_500ng_1FLuc_500ng_20mer-2_50ng_147mingrad-1      500ng
table(sheet$malat_load)
#> 
#> 125ng 250ng 500ng 
#>     8    12     7

Say which column is a factor and which level is the baseline. Everything else is mzLib’s:

design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "malat_dilution_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("malat_load", "500ng")),
                      out = file.path(tempdir(), "malat_design"))
stratum <- design$strata[["all"]]
stratum$column_names
#> [1] "intercept"        "malat_load=125ng" "malat_load=250ng"
c(rank = stratum$rank, aliased = length(stratum$aliased_terms), warnings = length(stratum$warnings))
#>     rank  aliased warnings 
#>        3        0        0
design$records[, c("contrast_id", "label", "estimability")]
#>   contrast_id                                label estimability
#> 1          c1 malat_load=125ng vs malat_load=500ng    estimable
#> 2          c2 malat_load=250ng vs malat_load=500ng    estimable
design$records$fitted_weights
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0 1 0
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 0 0 1
  • The columns are named factor=level. The reference comes first and has no column; the other levels follow in ordinal (character) order, so 125ng before 250ng. That is R’s model.matrix() with the same level order.
  • The default contrasts are each level against the reference. Each is one design column here, so fitted_weights has a single 1.
  • out wrote design_1.tsv, the design table stats_fit() reads, and contrasts_1.tsv, each estimable contrast’s weights on the same columns, which stats_fit(contrasts = ) reads.

Fit it. Each contrast against the reference is its design column, tested by name:

responses <- file.path(stats_data, "malat_dilution_log2_vs_fluc.tsv")
fit <- stats_fit(responses, stratum$design_file, c("malat_load=250ng", "malat_load=125ng"))
fit$status_counts
#>               fitted too_few_observations       rank_deficient 
#>                  212                  214                   66
malat <- fit$records[fit$records$status == "fitted" & startsWith(fit$records$feature, "MALAT1:"), ]
aggregate(estimate ~ coefficient, data = malat, FUN = median)
#>        coefficient   estimate
#> 1 malat_load=125ng -1.0144266
#> 2 malat_load=250ng -0.8914901

The same numbers as the hand-made design, because it is the same model: this package’s live tests hold the two fits equal, feature by feature.

Or test the contrasts file itself, and get a confidence interval with each answer. Name the coefficients too, and one call returns both tables:

both <- stats_fit(responses, stratum$design_file, c("malat_load=250ng", "malat_load=125ng"),
                  contrasts = stratum$contrasts_file)
both$contrasts$weights
#> $c1
#> [1] 0 1 0
#> 
#> $c2
#> [1] 0 0 1
c2 <- both$contrasts$records[both$contrasts$records$contrast == "c2", ]
coefficient <- both$records[both$records$coefficient == "malat_load=250ng", ]
identical(c2$t, coefficient$t)
#> [1] TRUE
row <- c2[c2$status == "fitted" & startsWith(c2$feature, "MALAT1:"), ][1, ]
row[, c("feature", "observed", "estimate", "confidence_low", "confidence_high")]
#>                  feature observed   estimate confidence_low confidence_high
#> 493 MALAT1:AAAAAAAAACUCG        4 -0.7533737      -3.681669        2.174922

A contrast of one column is that column’s test, number for number, so c2 repeats the malat_load=250ng rows and adds the interval. This oligo was measured in 4 runs, and its 95% interval cannot tell halving from no change. The contrasts file earns its keep for comparisons that are no single column, such as 250 ng against 125 ng: declare no reference level and diff_design() writes every pair, as the differential-abundance article shows.

Covariates, units and batch

A covariate is a number in a unit. Say the unit, and how the slope should read: here age in years, as a slope per decade, centred at 50 years. Batch is a fixed block. The sheet is mzLib’s own test design, and base R’s model.matrix() for it ships beside it:

design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "design_factor_batch_covariate_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "ctrl")),
                      covariates = list(covariate_spec("age", "years", scale = 10, scaled_unit = "decade",
                                                       centre = 50)),
                      batch = "batch")
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
#> [1] "intercept"         "condition=treated" "batch=b2"         
#> [4] "age (per decade)"
design$records[2, c("label", "covariate_unit", "covariate_scale")]
#>              label covariate_unit               covariate_scale
#> 2 age (per decade)         decade years/10, centred at 50 years
r_matrix <- as.matrix(read.delim(file.path(diff_data, "design_factor_batch_covariate_matrix.tsv"),
                                 check.names = FALSE))
colnames(r_matrix)
#> [1] "(Intercept)"      "conditiontreated" "batchb2"          "I((age - 50)/10)"
max(abs(unname(stratum$matrix) - unname(r_matrix)))
#> [1] 0

Every value equals R’s model.matrix(~ condition + batch + I((age - 50)/10)); this package’s tests also run model.matrix() here and compare.

Leave a field out and mzLib chooses. covariate_spec("age", "years") sends no scale, scaled unit or centre, so the slope is per year and the centre is the stratum’s mean; covariate_centres reports the centre used. Batch enters the model only when you name its column, and drops out with a warning in a stratum that has only one batch.

When the samples cannot answer

Here every sample of condition A ran in batch 1 and every sample of B in batch 2:

design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "design_confounded_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "A")), batch = "batch")
stratum <- design$strata[[1]]
stratum$column_names
#> [1] "intercept"   "condition=B" "batch=2"
c(rank = stratum$rank)
#> rank 
#>    2
stratum$aliased_terms
#> [1] "condition" "batch"
design$records[, c("label", "estimability")]
#>                        label             estimability
#> 1 condition=B vs condition=A not_estimable:confounded
is.null(design$records$fitted_weights[[1]])
#> [1] TRUE

No analysis of these samples can separate the condition from the batch, and mzLib says so instead of returning a number. The verdicts are "estimable"; "not_estimable:confounded", where the comparison lies along a direction two or more terms share, as here; and "not_estimable:rank_deficient", where it needs a column no sample informs, such as an interaction cell with no samples.

The design file still holds a design that can be fitted: fitted_column_names leaves out the later of two aliased columns, because a fit refuses a design without full rank. A contrast that is not estimable has no fitted weights (NULL), so it never reaches the contrasts file.

Strata: one design per tissue

When samples are different kinds of thing - liver and muscle - a comparison is made within each kind. Name the stratum column, and each stratum gets its own design:

design <- diff_design(file.path(diff_data, "stratified_samples.tsv"),
                      factors = list(factor_spec("condition", "A")), strata = "organism part")
lapply(design$strata, function(s) s$sample_ids)
#> $`organism part=kidney`
#> [1] "s7" "s8"
#> 
#> $`organism part=liver`
#> [1] "s1" "s3" "s5"
#> 
#> $`organism part=muscle`
#> [1] "s2" "s4" "s6"
design$strata[["organism part=kidney"]]$not_run
#>                        label         reason id
#> 1 condition=B vs condition=A not_in_stratum c1
design$records[, c("stratum", "contrast_id", "label")]
#>                stratum contrast_id                      label
#> 1  organism part=liver          c1 condition=B vs condition=A
#> 2 organism part=muscle          c1 condition=B vs condition=A

Kidney has only condition A, so there is nothing to compare there, and not_run says so: it skips c1, condition=B vs condition=A. A contrast id is numbered once over the whole analysis: c1 is the same comparison in liver and in muscle, and a stratum that cannot run it skips the id. With out, stratum i writes design_i.tsv, numbered in the order of strata, because a stratum key can hold characters a file name cannot.

From a peptide table to observations

diff_observations() reads the peptide table FlashLFQ (QuantifiedPeptides.tsv) or MetaMorpheus (AllQuantifiedPeptides.tsv) wrote, and needs the runs: which biological sample each file belongs to and, if it applies, its fraction and technical replicate. Grouping comes only from what you give here; mzLib never reads it out of a file name. This MetaMorpheus table is mzLib’s test data: three peptides in 18 runs, each run its own sample:

peptides <- file.path(diff_data, "MetaMorpheus_1.1.11_AllQuantifiedPeptides.tsv")
groups <- file.path(diff_data, "MetaMorpheus_1.1.11_AllQuantifiedProteinGroups.tsv")
header <- strsplit(readLines(peptides, n = 1), "\t")[[1]]
files <- sub("-calib$", "", sub("^Intensity_", "", header[startsWith(header, "Intensity_")]))
head(files, 2)
#> [1] "QE-002106_GM1_a" "QE-002107_GM1_b"
runs <- data.frame(file = files, sample = files)
observed <- diff_observations(peptides, runs, basis = "mbr_kept", protein_groups = groups)
observed
#> <mzlibr_observations> 3 peptides x 18 samples, mbr_kept
#>   quantified 8, mbr_transferred 1, ambiguous_peak 0, identified_not_quantified 0, not_detected 45
#>   normalization: none on 1 peptides

MetaMorpheus quantifies calibrated files, so its columns end in -calib; give the file name without it, and mzLib matches either. Each row is one peptide in one sample:

transferred <- observed$records[observed$records$state == "mbr_transferred", ]
transferred[, c("base_sequence", "sample", "log2_intensity", "unique_protein_group")]
#>    base_sequence          sample log2_intensity unique_protein_group
#> 10     CACASHVAK QE-002118_GM6_a       17.13515               Q16643
observed$records$state[is.na(observed$records$log2_intensity)][1]
#> [1] "not_detected"

basis decides whether match-between-runs values count, and mzLib has no default: it is your scientific choice. Under "msms_only" the same cell has no value, and still says why:

only <- diff_observations(peptides, runs, basis = "msms_only", protein_groups = groups)
same <- only$records[only$records$sample == "QE-002118_GM6_a" & only$records$base_sequence == "CACASHVAK", ]
same[, c("log2_intensity", "state")]
#>    log2_intensity           state
#> 10             NA mbr_transferred

The protein-group table adds each group’s q-value and flags. It is how a contaminant is recognised, and mzLib warns about groups the peptides name that it does not describe:

observed$protein_groups[observed$protein_groups$is_contaminant | observed$protein_groups$is_decoy, c("name", "genes")]
#>           name  genes
#> 4       P02769    ALB
#> 6 DECOY_P62750 RPL23A
observed$warnings
#> [1] "2 protein group(s) named by peptides are not in the protein-group table, so their q-value and decoy/contaminant status are unknown: Q16643, Q9UI26."

What each state means:

  • quantified: a value from MS/MS-identified peaks only.
  • mbr_transferred: the value includes a match-between-runs peak. Under "msms_only" it is left out, and log2_intensity is NA.
  • ambiguous_peak: a peak was found but withheld as ambiguous. No value.
  • identified_not_quantified: identified by MS/MS, but no peak could be quantified. No value.
  • not_detected: no value.

A sample whose runs disagree takes the most informative state among them. With fractions, mzLib sums a technical replicate’s fractions on the linear scale, then averages the sample’s replicates in log2: give runs fraction and technical_replicate columns.

Normalization, and the assumption it makes

diff_observations() always measures how far each sample sits from the others, and subtracts it only when you ask. mzLib’s rule: over the peptides with a value in every sample (decoys, contaminants and entrapments excluded), each sample’s shift is the median of its log2 value minus the peptide’s mean. Two runs of FlashLFQ’s E. coli spike-in vignette, which their names say were spiked at 1x and 2x:

spike_table <- file.path(diff_data, "EcoliSpikeIn_QuantifiedPeptides.tsv")
spike_runs <- data.frame(file = c("09-04-18_EcoliSpikeInSingleShot1x", "09-04-18_EcoliSpikeInSingleShot2x"),
                         sample = c("spike_1x", "spike_2x"))
spike <- diff_observations(spike_table, spike_runs, basis = "msms_only")
spike$normalization[c("setting", "reference_set_size")]
#> $setting
#> [1] "none"
#> 
#> $reference_set_size
#> [1] 86
spike$normalization$warnings
#> [1] "86 reference peptide(s) have a value in every sample and 86 in at least half, under the floor of 100, so no sample is shifted (none)."

Below mzLib’s floor of 100 shared peptides, nothing is shifted, because a median of a few peptides can move a whole sample by itself. You can lower the floor with min_peptides. Here is what that does on this table:

shifted <- diff_observations(spike_table, spike_runs, basis = "msms_only", min_peptides = 50,
                             normalize = TRUE, responses_out = file.path(tempdir(), "spike_in_responses.tsv"))
shifted$normalization$setting
#> [1] "shared_peptide_median"
round(shifted$normalization$shifts, 2)
#> spike_1x spike_2x 
#>    -0.47     0.47
by_peptide <- split(spike$records$log2_intensity, spike$records$full_sequence)
both_runs <- Filter(function(v) !anyNA(v), by_peptide)
c(peptides = length(both_runs), median_2x_minus_1x = round(median(sapply(both_runs, diff)), 2))
#>           peptides median_2x_minus_1x 
#>              86.00               0.94

The normalization removed the spike-in. This slice of the vignette holds almost only E. coli peptides, so nearly every peptide was doubled. The peptides measured in both runs sit close to one log2 unit higher in the 2x run, the doubling the names promise, and the two shifts take all of it away. Median normalization assumes most peptides do not change between samples. When most of them do - a table of the spiked organism alone, a loading series, a pull-down - that assumption is false, and normalizing deletes the result. Read the shifts before you subtract them.

responses_out also wrote the table’s own peptide-by-sample shape, which stats_fit() reads as its responses:

shifted$responses_written[c("row_count", "sample_count")]
#> $row_count
#> [1] 243
#> 
#> $sample_count
#> [1] 2

Its rows are peptides by full sequence, its columns the samples, and an empty cell means no value. For more than one stratum, narrow diff_observations() to one stratum’s samples with samples (a design file from diff_design() will do): the shifts are measured over every sample of the table, so measure each stratum on its own.

What these functions will not do

  • No protein roll-up and no row choice. mzLib does not yet turn the observation table into a protein-by-sample table, choose which rows a test uses (decoys, contaminants and q-value cuts included), or assemble fits into its differential result table. mzLibR does not do it either. Every peptide is a row; filter with protein_groups, unique_protein_group and the result’s protein_groups table.
  • Only the default contrasts. diff_design() lists each level against its reference (every pair when there is none) and each covariate’s slope. mzLib’s custom contrasts have no wire form yet; write your own contrasts file for stats_fit() instead.
  • The peptide table does not record FlashLFQ’s design, so mzLib cannot check that your runs group the files as FlashLFQ did. Give the runs the design FlashLFQ quantified with.
  • A table written in a comma-decimal locale does not read correctly. FlashLFQ writes in the machine’s culture, and mzLib reads with a decimal point.
  • mzLibR does no arithmetic. Every number on this page came from mzLib.

What to cite

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

  • doi:10.2307/2346786: the model-formula notation (main effects and a:b interactions) that R’s stats::model.matrix implements and mzLib’s design matrix equals (Wilkinson and Rogers, Appl Stat 22:392, 1973).
  • doi:10.1021/acs.jproteome.7b00608: FlashLFQ, whose peptide table and detection types this verb reads (Millikin et al., J Proteome Res 2018).
  • doi:10.1186/gb-2010-11-10-r106: the median-of-ratios idea the shared-peptide normalization follows: each sample against the log of a geometric-mean reference (Anders and Huber, Genome Biol 11:R106, 2010).
